passages.happening:
‘And the LORD said to Job’ (verse 1): “Will the faultfinder contend with the Almighty? Let him who argues with God give an answer” (verse 2).

‘Then Job answered the LORD’ (verse 3): “Behold, I am insignificant. How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth” (verse 4). He has spoken once, and twice, and he will add nothing more.
passages.hearers:
This short exchange stands between God's first and second speeches. Faultfinder, yissor, is found only here. It means one who corrects another, and the one doing the correcting has been Job. God's challenge carries a gentle irony: will the one who has been correcting the Almighty now answer?

Placing a hand over the mouth was a known sign of silence and respect before someone greater. Job himself described young men and princes doing it when he came to the city gate (29:9). Now he does it before God. In an honor culture it marks a decisive change: Job stops pressing his case.

He does not confess the sins the friends accused him of. He says he is small, and he falls silent.
passages.asks: Job put his hand over his mouth. Ask whether there is a time for you to stop arguing and be quiet before God. And ask whether that silence would be defeat, or something else.

passages.t: Would Job condemn God to justify himself?
passages.happening:
‘Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said’ (verse 6): “Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me. Would you really annul My justice? Would you condemn Me to justify yourself? Do you have an arm like God’s? Can you thunder with a voice like His?” (verses 7-9).

Then let Job put on majesty and splendor, honor and glory. Let him unleash his anger, look at every proud man and bring him low, trample the wicked where they stand and bury them in the dust. ‘Then I will confess to you that your own right hand can save you’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The second speech opens with the same words as the first. Then comes the question that names what went wrong in Job's speeches. Justice, mishpat, is the word that has run through the whole debate. Job complained that God denied him justice. Now God asks whether Job would cancel God's justice in order to be declared right himself.

Verses 10 to 14 draw on the picture of kingship in the ancient world. Kings were clothed in majesty, and one of their central duties was to bring down the proud and punish the wicked. God invites Job to take up that royal task over the whole world. If Job can do it, God will grant that Job's own right hand can save him. The right hand was the sign of strength and effective action. Justice across all creation is God's work, not Job's.
passages.hard:
Is God rebuking Job for protesting his suffering?

In part, yes, but the rebuke is carefully limited. God's question in verse 8 names what went wrong: in insisting that he was innocent, Job had drifted toward accusing God of injustice. God does not say Job was guilty of the sins the friends alleged, and he never takes back the prologue's verdict that Job was blameless. In chapter 42 God will say that Job spoke rightly of him, in contrast to the friends.

Interpreters reconcile these in different ways. Some say God rebukes Job's tone and overreach while approving his honesty. Others say God approves Job's refusal to accept false explanations, while correcting his demand that God answer to him. Either way, the book suggests that honest protest to God is not sin, but that it can cross into presuming to judge God. Job's response, silence and then repentance, is not a confession of the friends' charges. It is a recognition of who God is.
passages.asks: God asked Job whether he would condemn God to be proved right himself. Ask whether you have ever needed someone else to be wrong so that you could be right. And ask whether you have done that with God.

passages.happening:
“Look at Behemoth, which I made along with you. He feeds on grass like an ox” (verse 15). His strength is in his loins and the muscles of his belly. ‘His tail sways like a cedar’ (verse 17). His bones are tubes of bronze and his limbs rods of iron. ‘He is the foremost of God’s works; only his Maker can draw the sword against him’ (verse 19).

The hills bring him food, and the wild animals play nearby. He lies under the lotus, hidden among the reeds of the marsh, shaded by the willows of the brook. ‘Though the river rages, Behemoth is unafraid; he remains secure, though the Jordan surges to his mouth’ (verse 23). Can anyone capture him, or pierce his nose with a snare?
passages.hearers:
Behemoth is the plural of the ordinary word for beast, probably meaning the beast of beasts. God calls it the foremost of his works.

Made along with you is striking. Job and Behemoth are fellow creatures. The great beast that no one can master is God's handiwork, just as Job is.

Many scholars identify Behemoth with the hippopotamus: it eats grass, lies in marshes among reeds and lotus, is at home in rushing water and was famously hard to kill. Hippopotamuses lived in the Nile, and Egyptian art shows kings hunting them from boats. The mention of the Jordan need not mean the animal lived there; it may be a poet's way of naming any mighty, surging river.

The movement of the chapter is deliberate. From God's challenge to Job, the speech turns to a creature only God can master. Behemoth is an example of power beyond Job's reach.
passages.later: Behemoth's title, the foremost of God's works, echoes what wisdom says of itself: “The LORD created me as His first course, before His works of old” (Proverbs 8:22).
passages.hard:
What is Behemoth: the hippopotamus, a mythic beast, or something else?

Many scholars identify it with the hippopotamus, for the reasons above. Others have suggested the elephant or the water buffalo. Some interpreters, noting the heightened features, bones like bronze and a tail like a cedar, think it is a real animal described in mythic language, like the Leviathan of the next chapter. Some modern readers, especially young-earth creationists, have proposed that Behemoth was a dinosaur, pointing to the tail compared to a cedar; most scholars read that line as a poetic description of the hippopotamus's short tail or of another part of its body.

These notes take no side. On any reading the lesson is the same: here is a creature Job cannot capture or master, and God made it, and God made it along with Job.
passages.asks: God showed Job a beast no one could tame and said he made it along with Job. Ask what it does to you to be a fellow creature with the wildest things in the world. And ask what in your life you are trying to master that only God can.
